captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 7. In this lesson: The night train.
Use narrative tenses (past simple, past continuous, past perfect) to tell a story.
Here are some new words. Narrator. The person who tells the story. Carriage.
One of the separate parts of a train for passengers. Platform.
The place at a station where you get on a train.
And some more words. Glance. Look at something quickly. Anxious. Worried and nervous. Destination.
The place where you are going.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: the person who tells the story?
Now some grammar: Narrative tenses. Use the past simple for main events,
the past continuous for background actions and the past perfect for events that happened earlier.
For example: The train was moving slowly when I noticed the woman.
For example: I had never travelled alone before.
Now listen, and read along. The night train.
I had never travelled alone before, so I was anxious when Mum waved goodbye from the platform.
The train was already moving slowly into the dark. My carriage was almost empty.
An old man was sleeping by the window, and a woman in a green coat was reading a map.
I glanced at my ticket again: destination, Lakeside, 11.45 p.m.
Somewhere in the hills, the train shuddered and stopped. The lights flickered. Nobody spoke.
‘Don't worry,’ said the woman in the green coat. ‘A tree has fallen on the line. They'll clear it soon.
I've done this journey a hundred times.’
She was right.
Twenty minutes later we were moving again, and I realised that my hands had finally stopped shaking.
Another question. The video will stop. Why was the narrator anxious?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like narrator, carriage, platform. You practised narrative tenses.
And you read The night train. Now try the practice questions. See you next time!

captions: Hello, and welcome to Atomic English, Stage 7. In this lesson: A sense of place.
Describe a setting using expanded noun phrases and the senses.
Here are some new words. Setting. Where and when a story takes place. Atmosphere.
The feeling or mood of a place. Bustling. Full of busy, noisy activity.
And some more words. Deserted. Empty, with no people. Fragrance. A pleasant smell. Vivid.
Very clear and bright.
Time for a question. The video will stop. Which word means: where and when a story takes place?
Now some grammar: Expanded noun phrases.
Add adjectives before a noun and a prepositional phrase or relative clause after it to give more detail.
For example: a market becomes a bustling market with bright umbrellas.
For example: a street becomes a narrow, deserted street that smelled of rain.
Now listen, and read along. Morning in Lakeside. Lakeside woke up slowly. Mist hung over the still,
grey lake like a soft blanket, and the only sound was the slap of small waves against a wooden jetty.
By eight o'clock, the narrow main street had become a bustling market.
Stalls with striped umbrellas sold glossy red peppers,
baskets of warm bread and fish that had been caught an hour earlier.
The fragrance of coffee drifted from a tiny café whose blue door was always open.
Inside, an elderly man with a white beard was playing chess against himself.
Down by the water, a girl in yellow boots was feeding the ducks, laughing each time they splashed.
Another question. The video will stop. What was over the lake early in the morning?
Well done! Today you learned new words, like setting, atmosphere, bustling.
You practised expanded noun phrases. And you read Morning in Lakeside. Now try the practice questions.
See you next time!
